text.en:
Anita spilled a little soap solution on her yellow turmeric-stained handkerchief. The yellow turned red.
"Magic!" she said. Her teacher smiled. "No, chemistry. Turmeric changes colour in a base like soap."

Substances can be acidic, basic or neutral. Lemon juice, vinegar and tamarind are acidic and taste sour. Soap, baking soda and lime water are basic and feel slippery. Water and salt solution are neutral.
We use indicators to test substances. Blue litmus turns red in an acid. Red litmus turns blue in a base. Neutral substances do not change litmus. Turmeric turns red in a base. China rose gives a colour change too.
Never taste unknown substances. Acids and bases can be harmful, so handle them carefully and wash your hands afterwards.
Lemon, vinegar and tamarind are acids. They taste sour.
Soap and baking soda are bases. They feel slippery.
An indicator changes colour. Blue litmus turns red in an acid. Red litmus turns blue in a base.
Never taste an unknown substance. Handle it with care.

problem.en: Blue litmus paper dipped in lemon juice turns red. What does this tell us?

text.en: Blue litmus turns red only in an acid.
It turned red in lemon juice.

prompt.en: A friend says every liquid changes litmus colour. How will you correct this?

requiredIdeas.en: Neutral liquids such as pure water do not change litmus.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all liquids are acids or bases.

points.en: Acids are sour; bases are slippery; neutral substances change neither.
Indicators such as litmus show which is which.
